rationale: Both accounts describe the young king gathering a great force and campaigning against Judea, including Beth-zur; the surrounding accounts give different campaign years, and their troop totals are not harmonized.

Both narratives enumerate infantry, cavalry, and elephants for the royal expedition, but the numbers differ: 110000 infantry, 5300 horsemen and 22 elephants here, against 100000, 20000 and 32 in the companion account.
Menelaus's hope of recovering office continues the earlier portrayal of his obtaining the high priesthood by outbidding Jason and returning with a tyrant's disposition.
Menelaus's support for the invading king recalls his earlier role guiding Antiochus Epiphanes into the temple; the present expedition is under Epiphanes' son Eupator.
The royal condemnation of Menelaus as a cause of the evils reverses his earlier acquittal through Ptolemy's influence and continued office through the rulers' greed; the kings are different.

Menelaus dies without even a place in the earth, in contrast to the burial the Tyrians provided for the innocent representatives condemned while he was acquitted and retained office. The connection concerns their explicitly different final treatment, not merely the end of his career.

The narrator interprets Menelaus's death as recompense for offences against the altar; his earlier theft and sale of sacred gold provide a concrete account of his sacrilege, without equating those objects with the altar itself.
Eupator's intention to inflict worse evils than his father's recalls Epiphanes' slaughter in Jerusalem and profanation of the temple.

relationship: Prayer for endangered people and sanctuary
rationale: Judas orders prayer because people, law and temple are endangered, resembling the resistance's earlier appeal for help when holy places were profaned and the nations threatened destruction.
The plea not to fall again under blasphemous nations echoes the prayer at the temple's recovery not to be handed over again to blasphemous and barbarous nations.

The collective fasting and entreaty before assembling for war resemble the Mizpah preparations with prayer and fasting; here the observance lasts three days, while the companion passage reports fasting on the day of that assembly.
Judas's call to fight to the death for homeland and holy things resembles his exhortation before Emmaus that death in battle is preferable to witnessing the nation's and sanctuary's evils.

Both accounts describe royal pressure against Beth-zur and courageous resistance; the companion passage describes the defenders burning siege engines, whereas this passage summarizes the king's repulse.

Both accounts report the king negotiating with Beth-zur, but this passage has an exchange of pledges and departure, while the companion account describes evacuation for lack of provisions and a royal garrison.

News concerning Philip prompts a settlement in both accounts. Here Philip was left in Antioch and the king honours the temple; the companion account has Philip returning from Persia and Media and later records the king violating his oath by dismantling the wall.

Both accounts introduce the accession of Demetrius son of Seleucus; this account explicitly describes sailing to Tripolis with a strong force and fleet, whereas the companion account mentions departure from Rome and arrival at a coastal city with a few men.
Both narratives describe Antiochus and Lysias being killed as Demetrius takes the kingdom; the companion account narrates their seizure by the forces and Demetrius's refusal to see them.
The former high priest seeking access again to the altar corresponds to the Alcimus who leads the petitioners to Demetrius and wishes to serve as priest in the companion account.

Alcimus calls the Hasideans war-makers under Judas, while the companion narrative introduces them as strong warriors willingly devoted to the law; these are differing characterizations, not proof of identical membership at every stage.
Alcimus's claim that the Hasideans prevent stability contrasts with the companion narrative's specific report that Hasideans were first to seek peace from Alcimus and Bacchides.
Alcimus's statement that he has lost his ancestral priestly honour corresponds to the companion account's statement that he contended for the high priesthood.

relationship: Professed concern and disclosed motive; same-chapter
rationale: Alcimus claims concern for king and people, while the narrator has already disclosed his desire to regain access to the altar; the two passages distinguish his public justification from his personal stake.
Alcimus urges action on the ground that Judas prevents peace; the companion petition likewise accuses Judas and his brothers of ruining royal interests and asks the king to punish them.
Both narratives describe Demetrius sending Nicanor against Judas's people; the former elephant command and governorship are details supplied here.
The command to install Alcimus resembles the companion account's royal confirmation of his priesthood with military enforcement, although that passage commissions Bacchides, not Nicanor.
The earth sprinkled on Judas's men and their appeal for divine help repeat the concrete posture of supplication described before Timothy's attack; the opponents and campaigns differ.

relationship: Reluctance to fight and break peace; same-chapter
rationale: Nicanor's reluctance to settle matters by bloodshed is consistent with his later distress when ordered to annul the agreement with a man who had done no wrong.

relationship: Goodwill becomes the basis of accusation; same-chapter
rationale: Nicanor's attachment to Judas is precisely the goodwill Alcimus observes before accusing Nicanor of disloyalty to the king.
Both accounts have Alcimus return to the king with accusations against Judas's position; the claim about Nicanor's agreement and alleged appointment of Judas is particular to this account.

relationship: Royal order produces a capture plot; same-chapter
rationale: The order to send Judas in chains leads Nicanor to seek a stratagem and Judas to withdraw after noticing harsher treatment.
Nicanor's distress about annulling the settlement refers back to the accepted agreement, appropriate conference and continuing goodwill narrated earlier in the chapter.

Both accounts describe a plan to seize Judas under the cover of peaceful dealings; here the stratagem follows royal orders and a genuine settlement, whereas the companion account describes deceit from the initial approach.
Both accounts have Judas recognize danger in Nicanor's dealings and cease ordinary contact; the present account traces the change to the royal intervention rather than initial treachery.
Both accounts place Nicanor before the priests at the temple around the offering of sacrifices and connect his visit with the demand that Judas be surrendered.

Nicanor makes the temple's destruction conditional on failure to hand over Judas in both accounts; the proposed replacement temple for Dionysus is specified here, while the companion account threatens burning.
The hand stretched toward the temple while Nicanor threatens destruction is explicitly recalled when Judas displays the blasphemer's severed hand after the victory.
Both accounts follow Nicanor's threat with the priests appealing to God at the sanctuary; the companion prayer explicitly asks vengeance upon him and his army.

The priests affirm that the Lord needs nothing yet chose a temple among them, resembling Solomon's acknowledgment that even heaven cannot contain God while asking Him to hear prayer directed toward the chosen house.

relationship: God has no need of human service
rationale: The declaration that the Lord needs nothing corresponds to Paul's denial that God is served as though He needed anything; their statements about the temple occur in different arguments and are not made identical.
The plea to preserve the recently purified house refers to the narrated cleansing of the temple and restoration of worship on the twenty-fifth of Chislev.
The request to preserve the house undefiled is answered by the final thanksgiving that the Lord has preserved His own place undefiled.

relationship: Body and soul risked for ancestral faith
rationale: Razis's readiness to risk body and soul for Judaism resembles the martyr's declared surrender of body and soul for ancestral laws; the text does not identify Razis as one of that family.

Razis turns his sword on himself as enemies close in and he fears dishonour, resembling Saul's falling on his sword to avoid abuse by his captors; Razis survives this first wound and the subsequent course differs.

Razis's wish to die nobly rather than suffer degrading capture resembles Eleazar's choice of a glorious death rather than a defiled life; Eleazar submits to execution, while Razis inflicts his own wounds.

relationship: Restoration of bodily members hoped for
rationale: Razis asks the Master to give back the bodily organs he has lost, resembling the martyr's hope of receiving his sacrificed bodily members again from heaven; their deaths arise in different circumstances.
Nicanor's intended attack on the day of rest resembles Apollonius's earlier exploitation of the Jews' Sabbath rest before a massacre; the plans belong to different commanders and occasions.
The accompanying Jews appeal to the holiness God gave the day, directly corresponding to the command to sanctify the Sabbath and the statement that the Lord blessed and made it holy.
The declaration that the heavenly Lord commanded the seventh day's observance points to the law naming that day the Lord's Sabbath and grounding it in His rest after creation.
Nicanor's assertion of earthly authority to order armed service opposes the preceding appeal to God's command; Exodus identifies the seventh day as the Lord's Sabbath and prohibits work on it.
Nicanor plans a trophy over Judas's men, but the chapter ends with Nicanor's own head displayed as a visible sign of the Lord's help.

relationship: Battle exhortation grounded in divine help
rationale: Judas's command not to fear the advancing nations but expect divine help resembles the law's exhortation not to fear a larger enemy because the Lord fights for His people.

Judas encourages the fighters from the law and prophets, while the companion prebattle assembly unrolls the book of the law; the target neither names prophetic readings nor identifies the passages used here.
The reminder of foreign faithlessness and violated oaths recalls the king's command to annul Nicanor's settlement and Nicanor's consequent attempt to capture Judas by stratagem.

relationship: Former high priest in the vision
rationale: The virtuous former high priest Onias who appears in Judas's dream is the man whose unjust murder and admirable conduct the earlier narrative recounts; the vision is not a reversal of that reported death.

The vision presents Jeremiah as praying for the people and holy city; in the prophetic narrative the surviving people ask Jeremiah to pray for them and he agrees. The target describes his earthly ministry, not this dream.

relationship: Vision's assurance followed by victory; same-chapter
rationale: The dream's promise that Judas will shatter adversaries is followed by the narrated victory attributed to God's manifestation; the battle passage does not identify a physical sword as the dream's golden sword.

relationship: Battle for nation and holy places
rationale: The decision to face danger for the city and temple resembles Judas's earlier exhortation to fight the enemies threatening the nation and holy places, even at the cost of death.
The fighters' foremost fear for the temple responds to Nicanor's explicit threat to level its enclosure, tear down its altar, and erect a temple for Dionysus there.

relationship: Victory does not depend on weapons
rationale: Judas's confidence that victory does not come through weapons closely resembles David's declaration that the Lord does not save by sword and spear because the battle belongs to Him.
Judas again opposes confidence in weapons to confidence in divine power, the same distinction he made before the earlier campaign against Nicanor.
The prayer expressly recalls the Lord's angel killing 185000 in Sennacherib's camp, the event narrated before the Assyrian king's withdrawal.
The companion account of the prayer before Nicanor's defeat likewise recalls an angel striking 185000 after royal blasphemy; this account expressly names Hezekiah and Sennacherib.

relationship: Angel and terror before the people
rationale: The request for an angel to go before the army and bring terror resembles the law's promise of an angel going before Israel and fear confounding its enemies; the occasions are distinct.
Both versions of Judas's prebattle prayer ask God to crush the opposing army because of its blasphemy against the holy people or holy places.
Judas's men meet the enemy with invocation, corresponding to the companion narrative's placement of Judas's prayer immediately before the battle against Nicanor.

Both accounts narrate the destruction of Nicanor's army; the present account specifies at least 35000 struck down, while the companion account describes flight, pursuit and the army's destruction without that number.

Both narratives report Nicanor's death in battle; this account describes recognition of his armoured body after the engagement, while the companion account says he fell first and his men fled when they saw it.
Both accounts have Nicanor's head and right hand cut off and brought to Jerusalem for display; the inclusion of the shoulder is specified here.
The displayed hand is expressly identified as the one Nicanor stretched out against the temple while threatening its destruction in the previous chapter.
The thanksgiving that the Lord preserved His place undefiled answers the priests' earlier plea to preserve the recently purified house undefiled.
Both accounts describe public display of Nicanor's severed head at Jerusalem; this account specifically places it on the citadel, a location the companion passage does not specify.
Both accounts establish annual celebration of Nicanor's defeat on the thirteenth of Adar; the explanation that it precedes Mordecai's day is supplied here.

Both narratives close the Nicanor episode with a measure of security for the Jews; the companion text explicitly limits the land's quiet to a few days, whereas this author ends his account with the city held by the Hebrews.
The author's closing wish for a work well composed and to the point recalls his introductory commitment to concise expression rather than exhaustive treatment.
The closing analogy of mixed wine explains how the arrangement of the account delights its audience, returning to the introduction's explicit aim of pleasure and benefit for readers.
